A cognitive diagnostic model (CDM), also called a diagnostic classification
model, sorts examinees by which of a few skills, or *attributes*, they have
mastered. Each examinee belongs to one of $2^K$ latent classes, one for each
pattern of mastery of $K$ attributes. The latent variable is discrete, so it
sums out of the likelihood exactly: the log-posterior of the item parameters
and the class proportions has a closed form, and `inla_vanilla()` can take
it as it is.

This article fits the DINA model to a language test, and compares the
posterior marginals with those of Stan.

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(inlavanilla)
data(items_ecpe, qmatrix_ecpe, package = "edmdata")
```

## The data

The Examination for the Certificate of Proficiency in English (ECPE) data
(Templin & Hoffman, 2013), from the edmdata package, hold the right or wrong
answers of 2,922 examinees to 28 grammar items. A Q-matrix records which of
three attributes each item requires: morphosyntactic, cohesive and lexical
rules.

```{r}
#| label: data
y <- unclass(items_ecpe)
q <- unclass(qmatrix_ecpe)
dim(y)
head(q)
```

## The model

The $2^3 = 8$ classes are the rows of `alpha`, from no attribute mastered
(`000`) to all three (`111`). In the DINA model ("deterministic input, noisy
and gate"), examinee $i$ in class $c$ answers item $j$ correctly with
probability $1 - s_j$ if the class has every attribute the item requires
($\eta_{jc} = 1$), and with probability $g_j$ otherwise:

$$
P(y_{ij} = 1 \mid c) = (1 - s_j)^{\eta_{jc}} \, g_j^{1 - \eta_{jc}},
\qquad
p(y_i) = \sum_{c=1}^{8} \pi_c \prod_{j=1}^{28}
P(y_{ij} = 1 \mid c)^{y_{ij}} \{1 - P(y_{ij} = 1 \mid c)\}^{1 - y_{ij}}.
$$

The *guessing* and *slipping* probabilities $g_j$ and $s_j$ get uniform
priors, and the class proportions $\pi$ a Dirichlet(1) prior.

```{r}
#| label: classes
alpha <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(0:1), ncol(q))))
colnames(alpha) <- c("morphosyntactic", "cohesive", "lexical")
classes <- apply(alpha, 1, paste, collapse = "")
eta <- (alpha %*% t(q)) == matrix(rowSums(q), 8, 28, byrow = TRUE)
```

## The log-posterior

The probabilities go on the logit scale, and the class proportions on the
log-ratio scale against class `000`. Under a uniform prior the log-density of
$\text{logit}(g)$ is the log-Jacobian, $\log g + \log(1 - g)$. Under a
Dirichlet(1) prior the log-density of the log-ratios is $\sum_c \log \pi_c$.

```{r}
#| label: logpost
logpost <- function(theta, y, eta) {
  g <- plogis(theta[1:28])
  s <- plogis(theta[29:56])
  log_pi <- c(0, theta[57:63])
  log_pi <- log_pi - log(sum(exp(log_pi)))

  # Probability of a correct answer, items by classes
  p <- t(eta) * (1 - s) + t(!eta) * g

  # Log-likelihood of each examinee in each class, then summed over classes
  l <- y %*% log(p / (1 - p)) +
    rep(colSums(log1p(-p)) + log_pi, each = nrow(y))
  l_max <- l[cbind(seq_len(nrow(l)), max.col(l))]
  loglik <- sum(l_max + log(rowSums(exp(l - l_max))))

  loglik + sum(log(g) + log1p(-g) + log(s) + log1p(-s)) + sum(log_pi)
}
```

## The fit

There are 63 parameters: 28 guessing and 28 slipping parameters, and 7
class log-ratios.

```{r}
#| label: fit
init <- c(
  setNames(rep(qlogis(0.2), 28), sprintf("g%02d", 1:28)),
  setNames(rep(qlogis(0.1), 28), sprintf("s%02d", 1:28)),
  setNames(rep(0, 7), paste0("pi", classes[-1]))
)
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init, y = y, eta = eta)
```

Draws give the parameters on the probability scale, and the share of
examinees who have mastered each attribute, $\sum_c \pi_c \alpha_{ck}$:

```{r}
#| label: natural
natural <- function(theta) {
  log_pi <- c(0, theta[57:63])
  pi <- exp(log_pi) / sum(exp(log_pi))
  c(
    plogis(theta[1:56]),
    setNames(pi, paste0("pi", classes)),
    colSums(pi * alpha)
  )
}
set.seed(1)
draws <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 10000, fun = natural)
round(colMeans(draws[, 57:67]), 3)
```

Over two in five examinees have mastered all three attributes, and nearly a
third none of them. The classes with only the morphosyntactic or only the
cohesive attribute are rare, at 1 to 2%.

The fit takes about 40 seconds, most of it in the 70,000 or so calls of
`logpost` that 63 parameters need without a gradient.

## Checking against Stan

Stan samples the same model, with the classes summed out in the same way and
the same priors. Its 10,000 draws took about two minutes, after compiling
the model, and were summarised ahead of time
(`lab/cdm-article.R` in the package source), so this page does not need Stan
to build.

```{r}
#| label: reference
ref <- readRDS("cdm-stan.rds")
ref[c("rhat", "divergences")]
```

For each block of parameters, the largest gap between the posterior means,
in Stan's posterior SDs, and the range of the ratio of the SDs:

```{r}
#| label: compare
gap <- (colMeans(draws[, 1:64]) - ref$summary$mean) / ref$summary$sd
sd_ratio <- apply(draws[, 1:64], 2, sd) / ref$summary$sd
block <- rep(c("guessing", "slipping", "class proportions"), c(28, 28, 8))
data.frame(
  max_gap = tapply(abs(gap), block, max),
  sd_ratio_min = tapply(sd_ratio, block, min),
  sd_ratio_max = tapply(sd_ratio, block, max)
)[c("guessing", "slipping", "class proportions"), ] |>
  round(2)
```

The 56 item parameters agree to a few hundredths of a standard deviation.
The class proportions agree less closely where the classes are rare. Their
posteriors pile up against zero, which a skew-normal on the log-ratio scale
does not reach. The worst is `pi010`, the cohesive-only class: its mean is
0.23 SD high and its SD 13% narrow, a gap of 0.003 on the probability scale.
`summary(fit)` flags it, and the other two rare classes, with large ridge
bends. The class proportions, Stan in grey:

```{r}
#| label: densities
#| fig-height: 4
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
for (cl in paste0("pi", classes)) {
  d_ref <- ref$density[[cl]]
  d_iv <- density(draws[, cl], n = 256, from = 0)
  plot(
    d_ref$x, d_ref$y, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "grey75",
    xlim = range(d_ref$x[d_ref$y > max(d_ref$y) / 100]),
    ylim = c(0, max(d_ref$y, d_iv$y)), xlab = cl, ylab = "", yaxt = "n"
  )
  lines(d_iv, lwd = 1.5, col = "#B5772E")
}
par(op)
```

## Classifying examinees

Each examinee's chance of having mastered each attribute is a function of the
parameters, so draws of it average over their uncertainty. For the first
three examinees:

```{r}
#| label: mastery
mastery <- function(theta, y_i) {
  g <- plogis(theta[1:28])
  s <- plogis(theta[29:56])
  log_pi <- c(0, theta[57:63])
  p <- t(eta) * (1 - s) + t(!eta) * g
  l <- drop(y_i %*% log(p / (1 - p))) + colSums(log1p(-p)) + log_pi
  w <- exp(l - max(l)) / sum(exp(l - max(l)))
  colSums(w * alpha)
}
set.seed(1)
t(sapply(1:3, function(i) {
  colMeans(sampling(fit, nsamp = 1000, fun = mastery, y_i = y[i, ]))
})) |>
  round(3)
```

estimates using Mplus. *Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice*,
*32*(2), 37–50. <https://doi.org/10.1111/emip.12010>
